title: Microsoft Rayfin: Guide to Fabric Apps
summary: An independent explainer on Rayfin, an open-source SDK/CLI announced at Microsoft Build 2026 that provisions a governed, code-first application backend (SQL database, auth, GraphQL API, static hosting) directly onto Microsoft Fabric capacity, underpinning the broader Fabric Apps initiative.
audience: Developers and architects evaluating Fabric as an application backend platform rather than purely an analytics platform.
why_it_matters: Fabric Apps/Rayfin extends Fabric's remit from BI/analytics into transactional application backends, which is a meaningful capability-taxonomy expansion (touching sql-database, graphql-api, onelake) worth tracking even from a single unverified write-up, since the underlying product surfaces (GraphQL API, SQL Database item) are independently corroborated by Microsoft's own Fabric documentation.
takeaways: Rayfin is a code-first CLI/SDK, not a low-code tool — it targets professional developers and AI coding agents, positioned distinctly from Power Apps.

A single deploy command provisions three managed child services: a SQL Database with schema generated from TypeScript decorators, Entra ID authentication, and OneLake-connected static content hosting.
Application data lands in OneLake automatically as part of the deployment model, without a separate ETL step to get transactional data into the analytics estate.
The product was in public preview at the time of the post, with the author explicitly flagging that CLI syntax and APIs are subject to change before general availability.

Rayfin requires an active Fabric capacity (a minimum tier for development, a higher tier recommended for production) plus tenant-admin enablement, tying it into existing Fabric capacity administration.

claims.text: Rayfin is described as an open-source SDK and CLI, announced at Microsoft Build 2026, that provisions a complete application backend onto Microsoft Fabric capacity from a single command, underlying the broader Fabric Apps initiative.
Deploying a Rayfin application provisions a Fabric SQL Database whose schema is generated automatically from TypeScript decorator-annotated data model classes rather than hand-written DDL.
A Rayfin deployment exposes a GraphQL API endpoint automatically generated from the application's TypeScript data model, alongside a type-safe client SDK for consuming it.
Rayfin routes application data into OneLake as part of its managed deployment, without requiring a separate ETL pipeline to move transactional data into the analytics layer.
Row-level security policies for a Rayfin application's SQL Database are defined declaratively in TypeScript code alongside the data model, rather than configured separately after schema deployment.
Rayfin provisions an Entra ID-based authentication service as one of three managed child services (alongside the SQL Database and static content hosting) created by a single deployment.

Per the post, running a Rayfin application requires an active Fabric capacity, with a lower F-SKU tier suggested for development and a higher tier recommended for production, plus tenant administrator enablement in the admin portal.
The post positions Rayfin as targeting professional, code-first developers and AI coding agents, explicitly distinguishing it from Power Apps' low-code/citizen-developer model.
